summary.prose: Every operation the installed gh offers that a program can run without a person is reachable through a named, typed tool, and nothing new is a raw passthrough (the one existing raw input, gh_repo_clone.extraArgs, is kept for compatibility and makes the call destructive). The 46 existing gh tools keep their ids and meaning and gain typebox input and output schemas, a per-input approval class (closing, merging, deleting, every rename including a release's newTag, every visibility change, every overwrite flag and a clone with extra git arguments are destructive) and failure kinds. Each gh job has its own time limit from one table, never shorter than the tool has today, and a command that outlives it ends with a timed-out message naming the command and the limit; a change that began and did not finish cleanly is reported as having an unknown outcome. The operations gh has and the registry lacks are added as 22 family tools with an op input, the pattern git_branch and git_tag use, and a per-operation table gives each operation its exact inputs, requiredness (every selector gh needs to run without a prompt is required, and codespace create always passes --default-permissions so it never prompts), output and discriminator, approval class and limit, with an input inventory, a real-CLI parser check and a coverage table for what the user chose to leave out.

hldContextSlice.frameworkSummary: Alternative a1: the executor in src/daemon/tools/executor.ts becomes the one pipeline for all external operations, and git, gh and Jira (acli) are registry tool families with an optional declared output schema and an approval class (none, common or destructive). Workflow and daemon code call tools through a typed helper that takes the tool definition; about 32 production files that spawn git or gh, or call a wrapper that does, move onto it in one change.

consumedContracts.name: Tool output schema and typed call
consumedContracts.purpose: Lets a tool declare its result shape, has the executor check it when declared, and gives callers a result typed from the tool definition they pass.

consumedContracts.name: Text conversion with cross-check
consumedContracts.purpose: Turns text-only CLI output into the declared shape using the cheap model, cross-checks the key values against the raw text, and escalates once to a higher-tier model; conversions run serially.

consumedContracts.name: Approval class and approval exchange
consumedContracts.purpose: Defines the one field that gives a tool or call its approval class, the global setting that governs the common class, the request the executor sends to the attached client, the answer, the timeout and the denial reasons, so that every client implements the same exchange.

consumedContracts.name: CLI failure kinds
consumedContracts.purpose: One set of failure kinds returned by every git, gh and acli tool so callers tell a missing CLI, a missing sign-in, a time-out and a rejection apart.

boundary.internal: The list of gh operation families, their schemas (read from gh --json where it exists, converted from text otherwise, for example gh pr diff and gh run view --log), which of the 27 gh operations that need approval are in the destructive class, and the 120 second time limit and its message. Existing gh ids keep their meaning.

adjacentBoundaries.internal: The hook stage inside executeTool: the registry of hooks keyed by tool id, registration order, the rule that a hook runs only after a successful, checked call, and the way a hook failure is carried on the result. It places its stage at step 5 of the pipeline order in the architecture shape and does not own the schema check or the approval step.

The optional output-schema field and the check at step 4 of the pipeline, the typed call helper that takes a tool definition, the serial conversion queue, the key-value cross-check and the one-time escalation, and the shared failure kinds. It includes the choice of schema language and the way an input-to-tool mismatch is reported. It does not declare or read the approval class.

The approval step at step 2 of the pipeline: the single approval field on a tool definition, the global approval setting for the common class and its default, the IPC request and answer methods, the timeout value, the daemon-side holder of the pending requests, the terminal-client, editor and chat implementations of the answer, and removal of the 'auto-approving' fallback in executor.ts. It maps every existing requiresApproval flag, in every family, to the common class, and lists the tools that change. It does not choose which individual git, gh or Jira operations are destructive; each family Story marks its own.

The list of git operation families, their input and output schemas, which git operations are in the destructive class (for example force push, hard reset, clean, deleting a branch or tag), and the parsing of git porcelain output. Operations that need approval but cannot destroy work stay in the common class. Existing git ids keep their meaning.

The Jira tool families over acli (work item view, search, create, edit, transition, assign, comment, link, project list and view), their schemas, the --yes flag on every mutating command, the bounded forms of search and project list that acli requires, the 'acli jira auth status' sign-in check, and which operations are in the destructive class. An operation acli does not offer is left out and named as unsupported.

The repository check that fails on a direct git, gh or acli spawn outside src/daemon/tools, built first; the inventory it produces (about 32 production files known today, with the indexer, the design corpus reader, the analyze ignore filter, the understanding identity lookup and the daemon self-update included and no allowlist); the rewrite of every listed site and of the tests that import the old wrappers onto the typed helper; and the removal of runGit, commitAndPushArtifacts and the github.ts wrappers. It keeps the artifacts, commits and tracker records the same as before.
Private implementation of s8: Reach the rest of git through named, typed tools

nonFunctional.performance: gh commands time out after 120 seconds (decided with the user; the daemon is expected to become multi-threaded so a slow gh will not block it). The approval wait has its own timeout, set in s3's LLD. Conversion is serial, so a text-only tool that needs the cheap model costs one model call per attempt plus at most one escalated call; structured-output tools make no model call.
nonFunctional.security: No argument, setting, environment variable or caller identity can skip the approval for a destructive call; with no client attached the call is denied. Common calls follow one global setting. Approval requests travel only over the daemon's Unix socket. No credentials are read or stored: gh, git and acli use the user's own CLI sessions. A tool that declares an output schema and returns a result that does not match it fails and its result is not passed on. Today the executor runs every tool flagged requiresApproval as approved (11 git tools, 5 more by predicate, 27 gh operations and other families), so nothing asks; this Epic makes destructive calls ask every time and puts the rest under the global setting.
nonFunctional.observability: The executor logs each stage per call with the tool id, the caller, the approval class and decision and its reason, the schema check result, and each hook outcome. Hook failures, denials and conversion escalations are returned to the caller as part of the result, not only logged.
nonFunctional.durability: Pending approval requests are held in memory by the daemon and are lost on restart; a request left open at restart is treated as denied. Hooks are registered in code at start-up, not stored. The global approval setting is stored in the daemon's config. The cutover leaves artifacts, commits and tracker records unchanged.

api.signature: ghTimeoutMs(key: GhLimitKey): number  // GhLimitKey = { toolId: string; op?: string }

parameters.name: key
parameters.purpose: The tool and, for a family tool, the op

returns.meaning: The time limit in ms from the table in GhOpContracts for that job; a key with no row takes the class of its approval (read 30 s, write 60 s) so a new op is never unbounded

errors.condition: an unknown key takes the default class limit

api.name: ghExec
api.signature: ghExec(argv: string[], opts: { key: GhLimitKey; cwd?: string; input?: string; maxBytes?: number; cutIsAnswer?: boolean; hostname?: string; signal?: AbortSignal }): Promise<GhOutcome>

parameters.name: opts
parameters.type: { key, cwd?, input?, maxBytes?, cutIsAnswer?, hostname?, signal? }
parameters.purpose: The limit key, directory, optional standard input, the capture cap, whether a cut capture is the tool's documented truncated answer, the host the sign-in probe is scoped to, and the abort signal; no timeoutMs

returns.meaning: One normalised outcome: text stdout and stderr, code (null for a child ended by a signal), signal, spawnError, timedOut, stdoutTruncated, stderrOverflow, stdinError, aborted, the limit applied, the command text and, when the failure text was ambiguous, the exit code and output of one gh auth status --hostname probe made here

errors.condition: A spawn failure, a time-out, a stdin write error, a signal and a non-zero exit are fields of the outcome

postconditions: It always runs through runShellBytes, with or without input, because runShell reports neither stderrOverflow nor aborted; a byte-to-text adapter decodes stdout and keeps every runShellBytes field, and shell-helper.ts is not changed
No caller passes its own limit; the limit comes only from ghTimeoutMs
The input text never appears in argv

Standard-input delivery is known only as far as runShellBytes reports it: a stdin write error is stdinError, and gh's exit status carries the rest; a successful pipe write is not proof that gh read the value, and a failed one is not proof that gh did not act

api.name: ghFailureOf
api.signature: ghFailureOf(outcome: GhOutcome, opts: { mutating: boolean }): ToolFailure | undefined

parameters.name: outcome
parameters.purpose: What ghExec returned, including its probe

parameters.name: opts
parameters.purpose: Whether the call changes something, which decides whether a failure after execution began carries the unknown-outcome sentence

returns.meaning: undefined for a clean outcome. Otherwise the first matching row of this one precedence, whatever other flags are also set: (1) spawnError: missing-tool (execution never began); (2) timedOut: timed-out with 'gh <command> timed out after <limit> s'; (3) aborted: rejected; (4) signal set with no exit code (code null and signal set): rejected, naming the signal, even when stdinError or stderrOverflow is also set; (5) stdinError: rejected, even at exit 0; (6) stderrOverflow: rejected; (7) an unmarked cut capture (stdoutTruncated while cutIsAnswer is false): rejected; (8) non-zero exit: missing-signin only with authentication-specific evidence in the failing command's own text or in the probe's output (not logged in, authentication failed, bad credentials, token invalid or expired), unreachable for network text in either, otherwise rejected carrying gh's own error text; a probe that failed without authentication evidence stays rejected. For a mutating call, rows (2) to (6) happen after execution began and add the sentence 'the outcome is unknown; check the current state before retrying'; no message says that nothing changed or that a value was not set, and a plain non-zero exit (8) carries no claim about state. The probe's output is kept in failure.original

errors.condition: synchronous and total over every outcome, with the precedence above; the only subprocess it needs, the probe, was run by ghExec

postconditions: Each tool's existing failure text is kept in output and error; the kind is added beside it

api.signature: const GH_COVERAGE: readonly { command: string; owner: 'covered' | 'excluded'; toolIds?: string[]; op?: string; reason?: string }[]

returns.meaning: One row per gh group and subcommand of the installed gh, each served by a tool and op or excluded for a reason the user accepted

postconditions: A test fails when the installed gh lists a command with no row, when a covered row names a tool or op that is not registered, and when an excluded row has no reason

api.name: GH_INPUTS
api.signature: const GH_INPUTS: readonly { command: string; kind: 'flag' | 'positional' | 'synthetic'; name: string; field?: string; excluded?: string }[]

returns.meaning: One row per input of each covered gh command, of three kinds: a flag (name is the gh flag, read from the FLAGS section of `gh <command> --help`), a positional argument (name is the placeholder in the USAGE line, for example oldFilename in `gh gist rename {<id> | <url>} <oldFilename> <newFilename>`) and a synthetic field (a field the tool adds that is not a gh argument: op, cwd, repo where it is passed as -R, and any flag the tool always passes itself, such as --default-permissions on codespace create and --yes where gh has it). Each row names the input field that carries it, or the reason it is not offered (excluded)

postconditions: A test reads the flags from the FLAGS section and the positionals from the USAGE line of each covered command and fails when a flag or positional has no row; it fails when a row names a field that the op's input schema lacks; and it fails when a field of the op's input schema is accounted for by no row of any of the three kinds. op and cwd are synthetic rows of every op
A flag that is offered as a field in one op and excluded in another is checked per command, not globally

A safe real-CLI parser check builds each op's argv from a sample input whose value-taking flags carry representative values (the first enum member, the integer 1, the fixed --json field list, a placeholder string), appends --help as its own final token so no flag can consume it, and runs the installed gh with an empty temporary HOME and GH_CONFIG_DIR, no token and HTTPS_PROXY and HTTP_PROXY pointing at a closed local port; it asserts exit 0 and a USAGE section in the output, and fails on 'unknown flag' or any parse error, so a flag the installed gh does not know (including any flag the tool adds itself, such as --format) cannot pass. A command that executed instead of printing help would fail visibly and could not reach GitHub, and a canary case (gh issue delete 1 --help under the same conditions) must print help and make no request, which shows --help returns before the command body for the mutating ops too. The check proves flag validity only; constraints gh enforces when the command runs, such as release download needing a tag, a pattern or an archive, are carried by the schema's requiredness and tested by schema-rejection and argv tests

A prompt sweep fails when any op of the table can reach a gh prompt: an optional positional, or an optional selector flag, whose absence makes gh ask a person; each such input is required in the schema (the one choice between two forms, codespace delete's codespace or all, is exactly-one-of), codespace create always passes --default-permissions, and the integration test runs every op under a fake gh that exits with a failure if it sees a terminal prompt request; each prompt case in the table comes from the installed gh's help, not from the fake

dataModelChanges.details: A typebox output schema for each of the 46 existing tools and each op of the new tools. Existing list tools keep the data they return today and the schema describes it in place: repo list {count, repos}, run list {count, runs}, workflow list {count, workflows}, gh_pr_diff {number, diffBytes, truncated}, gh_run_view {runId, jobs} (with truncated added), the others as found when the tool is converted. New tools follow GhOpContracts, where every output carries the literal op.

NOTATION. Format: tool.op [class limit-seconds] inputs => output. Inputs: a bare name is required; name? is optional; a|b means exactly one of the two is given; a/b means not both; every op also takes cwd? and every -R op also takes repo? (OWNER/NAME, default from the working directory); ops marked (no -R) take no repo field. NO PROMPTS AND NO UNRUNNABLE INPUT: an input whose absence makes gh ask a person to choose, or makes gh refuse to run, is required, and a flag that suppresses a prompt is always passed by the tool, so no op can reach a prompt. TYPES: a field that carries a value-less gh flag is boolean; a repeatable flag or a list is string[]; limit, days, port, count and ids that gh documents as exact numbers are integers; a search qualifier that gh documents as a number, a size or a date accepts comparisons and ranges (for example >100, 10..50, >=2024-01-01) and is a string holding that expression; every other field is a string, and a field documented as {a|b|c} is that enum. OUTPUTS: every output has the literal property op equal to the input op (the discriminator of the output union). A list read with --json returns {op, count, items} where items have exactly the --json fields named. A list read from tab-separated text returns {op, count, rows} where rows is string[][] (the tab-split lines, no named columns), except gist list, whose columns id, description, files, visibility, updated were verified and which returns items with those five string properties. A text read returns {op, text}. A mutation returns {op, ok, target, message} (target the object or URL gh printed or the input identifier, message the trimmed stdout). A tool never passes --web, --follow, --show-token or --expand, never passes --json, --jq or --template except to set its own fixed --json fields, and never prompts: confirmation prompts are answered by the tool's own --yes where gh has one, which is a synthetic row. The tool adds only flags that the installed gh accepts for that command, and the parser check proves it. OVERWRITE RULE: an op whose purpose is create-or-update is common; a flag whose only purpose is to overwrite existing data (force, clobber) makes the call destructive; every rename (including label edit with newName and release edit with newTag), delete, transfer, close, logout and visibility change is destructive. gh_issue_manage (-R): status [none 30] => {op, createdBy, assigned, mentioned}, each an array of items with assignees,author,labels,number,state,title,updatedAt,url; delete [destructive 30] number; develop [common 60] number, name?, branchRepo?, base?, checkout?; develop-list [none 30] number => {op, count, rows}; lock [common 30] number, reason? EXISTING IDS keep these classes and limits: reads none 30 s: gh_issue_list, gh_issue_view, gh_pr_list, gh_pr_view, gh_pr_checks, gh_pr_files, gh_run_list, gh_workflow_list, gh_release_list, gh_release_view, gh_repo_view, gh_repo_list, gh_project_list, gh_project_view, gh:project:item-list, gh:project:field-list; gh_pr_diff and gh_run_view none 60 s. Common: gh_issue_create 60 s; gh_issue_comment, gh_issue_edit, gh_issue_reopen, gh_issue_link, gh_pr_edit, gh_pr_comment, gh_pr_review, gh_pr_ready, gh_run_rerun, gh_run_cancel, gh_release_publish, gh:project:item-add, gh:project:item-update, gh:project:item-archive 30 s; gh_release_edit 30 s, destructive when newTag is set (it renames the release's tag); gh_pr_create 90 s; gh_workflow_run 60 s; gh_release_create 180 s; gh_repo_create and gh_repo_fork 120 s; gh_repo_clone 600 s, destructive when extraArgs is non-empty (the existing string[] input forwarded after -- to git clone, where a flag such as --upload-pack can run a command; it stays for compatibility as a listed exception to the no-raw-argument rule and the user's accepted decision of 2026-10-25). Destructive: gh_issue_close, gh_pr_close, gh_release_delete, gh_repo_delete, gh:project:item-delete 30 s; gh_pr_merge 180 s. The input inventory test (GH_INPUTS) and the parser check are the build-time checks that these field lists and the flags the tools add match the installed gh.

GH_INPUTS lists, for every input of every covered gh command, one row of one of three kinds: flag, positional or synthetic. Not offered, with their reason: --web (opens a browser), --follow (streams until stopped), --show-token (prints a credential), --expand (evaluates remote file names as a Bash expression: a remote-execution path), gist edit --filename and the content of an existing gist file (need an editor), --json, --jq and --template (the tools set their own output form), --yes (the tool answers the prompt itself), and prompts. Always passed by the tool as a synthetic row: --default-permissions on codespace create, --yes where gh has it. The flags of each command are read from `gh <command> --help` and the positionals from its USAGE line by the inventory test, which compares them with the op's input schema fields and with the rows, so an input that is neither a field nor listed fails, as does a field that no row accounts for. op, cwd and repo are synthetic rows. The existing gh_repo_clone.extraArgs is the one recorded exception to the no-raw-argument rule; the no-passthrough test exempts exactly that field.

The mutating tools already declare approval 'common' as a fixed field (27 of them, set by s3). This Story replaces the field with ghApprovalClass where a class depends on the input and raises every close, merge, delete, transfer, rename, logout, visibility change and overwrite flag to destructive, among the existing tools gh_issue_close, gh_pr_close, gh_pr_merge, gh_release_delete, gh_repo_delete and gh:project:item-delete, and makes gh_release_edit (newTag) and gh_repo_clone (extraArgs) destructive per input. approval-class-mapping.test.ts changes too: its loop asserts tool.approval === 'common' for every former requiresApproval-true tool except an explicit PER_INPUT_SINCE_S4 set, so those eight join a new explicit PER_INPUT_OR_DESTRUCTIVE_SINCE_S5 set whose members must resolve to common or destructive and never none; the 228-row snapshot is not edited; the s5 tools and classes go in an addedByS5 list read beside addedByS4; the converted typebox input schemas are written so their JSON equals the snapshot's, as s4 did for git, and any unavoidable difference is listed in an explicit S5 schema exception list in the test, never by rewriting the snapshot; old-input compatibility is tested separately in gh-compat.test.ts from schema serialisation identity.

{ command, owner: covered | excluded, toolIds?, op?, reason? }. The excluded rows are the list the user accepted in chat on 2026-10-25 (docs/plans/tool-registry.md, 's5 decisions'): browse; auth login, refresh, setup-git and token; codespace ssh, code, jupyter and ports forward; run watch; api (a raw passthrough); completion; all of alias; config set and clear-cache; extension browse, install, remove, upgrade, create and exec. They need a person, a browser or a terminal, run or fetch code, change gh itself or print a credential. auth logout, auth switch, codespace cp, logs and ports were added at the user's request. The user also accepted, in the second set of decisions on 2026-10-25, the exclusion of replacing the content of an existing gist file (gh gist edit needs an editor) and of codespace cp --expand (a remote shell evaluation).

Today the default is 30 s and ten calls pass their own: run logs and workflow run 60, issue create 60, pr diff 60, pr create 90, pr merge 180, repo create and fork 120, repo clone 600, release create 180. After the change no call passes a limit; ghTimeoutMs gives each job the limit in GhOpContracts, never lower than today's, and the timed-out message names the command and the limit. A test fails when any ghExec call outside the table passes its own timeout.

interactionWithShared.howDetails: Each gh tool declares typebox inputSchema and outputSchema; the executor checks both; withGhFailureNet keeps the concrete definition so callTool types its input and result.

gh pr diff, gh run view --log and the free-text reads of gh_auth status, gh_status and gh_ruleset list go through convertText with keyValues cross-checked against the raw text; tab-separated reads and gh_config list use a deterministic parser and make no model call.

Each gh tool sets the approval field to ghApprovalClass or a fixed class; destructive calls ask every time. The field of a secret value is named secretValue, so the existing key mask in approval-policy.ts hides it. The key text of gh_ssh_key and gh_gpg_key add is a public key: a field named key is not masked by that policy and is shown in the approval request up to the existing 2000-character display limit (a longer string shows its first 2000 characters and its length). A tool-specific notice, such as the one for codespace create, goes in the preview title and content the tool supplies through buildApprovalGate, because the request reason is built by approval-policy.ts. The mask, the limit and the reason text are not changed here because sc4 is owned by s3.
ghFailureOf attaches failure.kind from the shared kinds; a conversion failure carries the raw text in failure.original.

errorCases.scenario: gh is not installed or cannot be spawned
errorCases.detection: ghExec gets a spawnError from runShellBytes and sets it on the outcome; ghFailureOf maps it first
errorCases.response: failure.kind missing-tool; error text names gh; execution never began, so this is the one failure that may say nothing changed
errorCases.userImpact: The call fails at once with a message to install gh

errorCases.scenario: gh is not signed in or the token is expired
errorCases.detection: The failing command's stderr, or the output of the one gh auth status --hostname probe ghExec ran, holds authentication-specific text (not logged in, authentication failed, bad credentials, token invalid or expired)
errorCases.response: failure.kind missing-signin with the probe output kept in failure.original
errorCases.userImpact: The user is told to run gh auth login outside the registry

errorCases.scenario: The network is unreachable or the host cannot be resolved
errorCases.detection: stderr or probe output matches network text (could not resolve host, connection refused, timeout dialing)
errorCases.userImpact: The call fails; a retry later can succeed, after a mutating call's state is checked

errorCases.scenario: A command outlives its per-job limit
errorCases.detection: runShellBytes reports timedOut; the outcome carries the limit applied from ghTimeoutMs
errorCases.response: failure.kind timed-out, text 'gh <command> timed out after <limit> s'; for a mutating call the text adds that the outcome is unknown and the state must be checked before retrying
errorCases.userImpact: The user learns which command and limit, and for a mutation must check the state before retrying

errorCases.scenario: A mutating call fails after execution began: an abort, a child ended by a signal (code null and signal set, whatever other flags are set), a stdin write error (secret, variable, key adds) or a stderr overflow
errorCases.detection: runShellBytes reports aborted, a signal with a null code, stdinError or stderrOverflow; the one precedence is timedOut, aborted, signal, stdinError, stderrOverflow, so a signal together with a stdin error is reported as the signal and a stdin error together with an overflow as the stdin error; none of them shows what the remote service did before the local failure
errorCases.response: failure.kind rejected with the sentence 'the outcome is unknown; check the current state before retrying'; the message never says the value was not set or that nothing changed; the secret value is never placed in argv or in the error text
errorCases.userImpact: The caller verifies the secret, variable or key with the matching list op before retrying; the value is not leaked

errorCases.scenario: A mutating call exits with a plain non-zero status and gh's own error text
errorCases.detection: runShellBytes reports a non-zero code with no timeout, abort, signal or stdin error
errorCases.response: failure.kind rejected carrying gh's error text and no claim about state

errorCases.scenario: A call carries a field the op's gh command does not accept, a missing required field (including any selector whose absence would make gh prompt or refuse to run, such as none of tag, pattern and archive on a release download), two fields of an exclusive pair, a field outside its enum, or an op the family does not offer
errorCases.detection: The op's input schema in GhOpContracts rejects it before any process starts
errorCases.userImpact: The caller corrects the input; nothing ran and no prompt can appear

errorCases.scenario: A caller asks for codespace cp with expand, a gist file's content to be replaced, a codespace create with its own permissions choice, or any other input that is not offered (web, follow, show-token)
errorCases.detection: The input schema has no such field, so the check rejects it before any process starts
errorCases.userImpact: No remote shell evaluation, no editor session and no permission prompt is reachable through the tool

errorCases.scenario: A tool would pass a flag the installed gh does not know (a version change, or a flag the tool adds itself such as --format or --default-permissions)
errorCases.detection: The real-CLI parser check builds the argv with representative values, appends --help as its own final token, and the installed gh reports an unknown flag or a parse error
errorCases.response: The test fails, naming the op and the flag
errorCases.userImpact: The defect is found at build time, not by a failed call

errorCases.scenario: A capture is cut at the cap for a tool that does not treat a cut as its answer
errorCases.detection: runShellBytes reports stdoutTruncated or stderrOverflow while cutIsAnswer is false
errorCases.response: failure.kind rejected rather than a silently partial success
errorCases.userImpact: The caller is told the output was incomplete

errorCases.scenario: sc3 conversion fails the key-value cross-check after one escalation
errorCases.detection: convertText returns a value whose key values are missing from the raw text
errorCases.response: failure.kind conversion-failed with the raw text in failure.original
errorCases.userImpact: The caller still has the raw text

errorCases.scenario: An exception is thrown inside a tool's execute
errorCases.response: A failure result with failure.kind, never a throw
errorCases.userImpact: The caller always gets a typed result

errorCases.scenario: The user declines the approval for a destructive call
errorCases.detection: The sc4 approval exchange returns a decline

edgeCases.input: gh_pr_diff or gh_run_view output larger than the tool's display cap
edgeCases.expected: A cut at the cap is a success with truncated true; the kept prefix runs to the cap, which can differ from the legacy runShell answer by up to one chunk

edgeCases.input: A secret set with envFile and also with name
edgeCases.expected: Rejected: exactly one of name and envFile is given

edgeCases.input: gh_release_asset download with none of tag, pattern and archive
edgeCases.expected: Rejected by the schema, because without a tag gh requires --pattern or --archive; with only a tag, only a non-empty pattern list or only an archive it is accepted

edgeCases.input: gh_repo_manage set-default with none of repository, view, unset, or with two of them
edgeCases.expected: Rejected: exactly one is required, so gh never prompts

edgeCases.input: gh_auth logout or switch with only hostname or only user
edgeCases.expected: Rejected: both are required, so gh never selects by prompt

edgeCases.input: gh_codespace create for a repository whose devcontainer requests additional permissions
edgeCases.expected: The generated argv always contains --default-permissions, so gh does not ask; the preview content the tool supplies states that the requested permissions are accepted; the fake gh fails the create if the flag is missing

edgeCases.input: gh_codespace delete with codespace, or with all, or with both or neither
edgeCases.expected: Exactly one of codespace and all is accepted; the prompt sweep treats this pair as the one allowed alternative, not as an optional selector

edgeCases.input: gh_repo_manage edit with visibility set
edgeCases.expected: Class is destructive; without visibility it is common; the generated argv contains --visibility and no confirmation flag

edgeCases.input: gh_project_manage link or unlink
edgeCases.expected: The generated argv has no --format; the ops that accept --format get it; the result is {op, ok, target, message}

edgeCases.input: gh_search with reactions set to '>100', comments to '5..20', created to '>=2024-01-01'
edgeCases.expected: Accepted as expression strings and passed through unchanged as the qualifier value; an integer-only schema would have rejected them

edgeCases.input: release upload or download with clobber true
edgeCases.expected: Class destructive; without clobber it is common

edgeCases.input: label create or clone with force, pr checkout with force, repo sync with force, codespace delete with force
edgeCases.expected: Class destructive

edgeCases.input: gh_gist rename, gh_repo_manage rename, gh_label edit with newName, or the existing gh_release_edit with newTag
edgeCases.expected: Each resolves to destructive, since every rename is destructive; label edit without newName and release edit without newTag are common; the test pins each resolved class

edgeCases.input: the existing gh_repo_clone with a non-empty extraArgs, for example --upload-pack=cmd
edgeCases.expected: Class destructive, so the user sees the arguments before git runs; with no extraArgs it is common; extraArgs stays in the schema and is the one recorded exception to the no-raw-argument rule

edgeCases.input: gh_ssh_key or gh_gpg_key add with key text longer than 2000 characters
edgeCases.expected: The approval request shows the first 2000 characters followed by the length, as approval-policy.ts does for every long string; key text up to 2000 characters is shown whole; keyFile shows only the path; a secretValue in the same request is masked

edgeCases.input: gh_gist edit with no add, remove or desc
edgeCases.expected: Rejected: at least one is required

edgeCases.input: An op string the family does not offer, or an unknown op reaching ghApprovalClass
edgeCases.expected: Rejected by the schema; ghApprovalClass returns destructive so it would ask

edgeCases.input: A gh version that lists a command, flag or positional with no GH_COVERAGE or GH_INPUTS row
edgeCases.expected: The coverage tests fail, naming the command or input

edgeCases.input: gist rename, which has three positionals and no flags
edgeCases.expected: GH_INPUTS has three positional rows, and op and cwd synthetic rows; the inventory test accounts for every schema field

edgeCases.input: A tool id or op missing from the time-limit table
edgeCases.expected: ghTimeoutMs gives the class default (read 30 s, write 60 s), never unbounded

edgeCases.input: gh list command that prints tab text off a terminal
edgeCases.expected: The deterministic tab parser returns rows as string arrays, or the verified gist columns; no model call

edgeCases.input: Output containing non-UTF-8 bytes
edgeCases.expected: The byte-to-text adapter decodes stdout with replacement; the fixture for a cut crossing a multibyte character must still yield valid text

edgeCases.input: release download with output set to '-'
edgeCases.expected: Rejected: output to standard output would be captured as the answer

migration.stateBefore: 46 gh tools in seven files under src/daemon/tools/builtins/gh/. ghExec in helpers.ts has a 30 s default and a 4 MiB capture cap; 47 calls, ten pass their own limit (60 s to 600 s). 27 mutating tools declare approval 'common' as a fixed field and none is destructive; gh_release_edit renames a tag through newTag and gh_repo_clone forwards a raw extraArgs list to git clone, both under common. No tool declares typebox input or an outputSchema. shellFail keeps only stderr text and drops the spawn, time-out and truncation flags. gh_pr_diff returns data {number, diffBytes, truncated}; gh_run_view returns {runId, jobs} and succeeds with stderr as the log body when the log command fails. Many gh operations (secrets, variables, labels, gists, codespaces, search, auth and the rest) have no tool.
migration.stateAfter: The 46 existing tools keep their ids, input meaning and result data, and gain typebox input and output schemas, per-input approval classes (close, merge, delete, transfer, every rename including a release's newTag, logout, visibility changes, overwrite flags and a clone with extraArgs destructive), failure kinds and a per-job time limit from one table that is never below today's. 22 family tools with an op input cover the rest of gh, each output carrying the literal op, no op able to reach a gh prompt or accept an input gh cannot run (codespace create always passes --default-permissions; release download needs a tag, a pattern or an archive), and every flag a tool adds checked against the installed gh by a parser check that runs --help with representative values. GH_COVERAGE and GH_INPUTS record every command and every flag, positional and synthetic input as covered or excluded with a reason, and tests check them against the installed gh. A mutating call that fails after execution began reports an unknown outcome under one precedence. gh_run_view gains the additive field truncated and now fails when its log command fails.

migrationSteps.action: Add the shared pieces: the limit table and ghTimeoutMs, the byte-to-text adapter over runShellBytes, ghExec with the key option and the one sign-in probe, GhOutcome, ghFailureOf (with its one precedence and the unknown-outcome rule for mutating calls), withGhFailureNet and ghApprovalClass. Existing tools are not touched yet.

Convert the existing tools file by file (issue, pr, repo, release, actions, project): typebox input written to serialise identically to the snapshot, output schema describing today's data, limit passed through the key instead of a number, fixed approval replaced by ghApprovalClass where the class depends on input, the six destructive tools raised, and gh_release_edit (newTag) and gh_repo_clone (extraArgs) made destructive per input. Update approval-class-mapping.test.ts with the PER_INPUT_OR_DESTRUCTIVE_SINCE_S5 set and addedByS5 list; the snapshot is not edited.

Change gh_pr_diff and gh_run_view to the cut-is-answer capture and the sc3 conversion; add truncated to gh_run_view and make a failed log command fail the call. This is the one visible behaviour change besides the stricter approval and is covered by fixtures that cross the cap and a multibyte character.
Add the 22 family tools with their op tables, the tab and config parsers and the stdin delivery for secret, variable and key adds, the codespace create preview notice, and register them in index.ts.

Add GH_COVERAGE and GH_INPUTS and the coverage, input, prompt-sweep, real-CLI parser, timeout, approval, failure and compatibility tests, with the fake gh binary fixture; record the performance amendment and update docs/plans/tool-registry.md.

migration.backwardCompat: Existing tool ids, input fields and result data are unchanged; the schemas serialise identically to the 228-row snapshot apart from any listed S5 exception, and gh_repo_clone.extraArgs and gh_release_edit.newTag stay. Approval is stricter for eight tools (close, merge and delete now destructive and ask every time; a release edit that sets newTag and a clone that sets extraArgs ask too), so a caller that relied on the common class now sees a prompt. Limits only grow or stay. gh_run_view gains the additive truncated field and now fails when its log command fails; a cut capture keeps the prefix up to the cap, so text and diffBytes at the cap can differ from today by up to one chunk. Failure text stays in output and error with failure.kind added beside it.

gpg-key list and ssh-key list return untyped rows because gh does not document their columns and the sign-in here lacks the scopes to list them; a later change can name the columns once they are verified.

codespace create always accepts the permissions the devcontainer requests (--default-permissions), and the notice is in the approval preview content; confirm this is acceptable, since the alternative would be to refuse codespaces that request extra permissions.
